```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

# Package versions are pinned via renv (see renv.lock); run renv::restore() to install.
# Functions are called with explicit pkg:: prefixes rather than attaching via library().

# Headline numbers used in the Summary. The price shock is written by the export-price-shock
# chunk below; the land-use results by r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R.
shock_2035 <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"))
lum <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_country_results.csv.gz"))

# Soybean oil's share of soybean crush value (Janzen & Wang 2025; see Methods). Must match
# SOY_OIL_VALUE_SHARE in r/land_use_model/01_prepare_data.R and 00d_supply_curve.R.
soy_oil_value_share <- 4.72 / (4.72 + 8.66)

# Additional forest loss relative to BAU: BAU stock minus scenario stock, so positive = more loss.
bau <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "bau") |>
  dplyr::select(country, year, carbon_bau = forest_carbon_tco2, area_bau = forest_area_ha)
loss <- lum |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_model", "vo_rs_palm", "vo_rs_soy")) |>
  dplyr::inner_join(bau, by = c("country", "year")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    carbon_loss = carbon_bau - forest_carbon_tco2, # t CO2
    area_loss = area_bau - forest_area_ha # ha
  )
global_loss <- loss |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    dplyr::across(c(carbon_loss, area_loss, carbon_bau, area_bau), sum),
    .by = c(scenario, year)
  )
gl <- function(scn, yr, var) global_loss[[var]][global_loss$scenario == scn & global_loss$year == yr]

final_year <- max(lum$year)
n_years <- final_year - min(lum$year)
country_final <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year == final_year) |>
  dplyr::mutate(share = carbon_loss / sum(carbon_loss), .by = scenario) |>
  dplyr::arrange(scenario, dplyr::desc(carbon_loss))
rs_final <- country_final |> dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs")
# Countries whose additional loss peaks and then narrows by >5% (BAU later clears some of the
# same forest), among those with more than 1 Mt CO2 of additional loss.
gap_peaks <- loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario == "vo_rs") |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    peak = max(carbon_loss),
    peak_year = year[which.max(carbon_loss)],
    final = carbon_loss[year == final_year],
    .by = country
  )
n_narrowing <- sum(gap_peaks$peak > 1e6 & gap_peaks$final < 0.95 * gap_peaks$peak)
mys <- gap_peaks[gap_peaks$country == "Malaysia", ]

# ILUC carbon intensity: additional forest carbon loss after T years of fuel use, divided by T
# years of VO-RD energy at the 2035 level. Annual VO-RD energy is ICCT's 2035 VO-RD share of
# shipping energy (Table 1), saved by the scrape-icct-table-1 chunk below.
icct_saved <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"))
icct_2035 <- icct_saved[icct_saved$year == 2035, ]
vord_mj_2035 <- icct_2035$vord_pct_energy_demand / 100 * icct_2035$shipping_energy_demand_ej * 1e12
vord_direct_ci <- 42.3 # g CO2e/MJ, soy VO-RD (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 6)
fossil_baseline_ci <- 93.3 # g CO2e/MJ, 2008 baseline (Seber & Pavlenko 2025, p. 1)
accounting_years <- c(20, 25, 30)
headline_years <- 25
iluc <- expand.grid(
  scenario = c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_model"),
  years = accounting_years,
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
iluc$carbon_loss <- mapply(
  function(scn, yrs) gl(scn, min(lum$year) + yrs, "carbon_loss"),
  iluc$scenario, iluc$years
)
iluc$g_per_mj <- iluc$carbon_loss * 1e6 / (iluc$years * vord_mj_2035)
iluc <- iluc[order(iluc$scenario, iluc$years), ]
il <- function(scn, yrs) iluc$g_per_mj[iluc$scenario == scn & iluc$years == yrs]
# Where an ILUC value sits relative to ICCT's 62 and Chen et al.'s 84.1 g CO2e/MJ, for the text.
vs_benchmarks <- function(x) if (x < 62) "below both" else if (x > 84.1) "above both" else "between them"

# Crop attribution: palm-only and soy-only runs of the Roberts & Schlenker shock. They sum to the joint run
# to within the interaction term reported here.
crop_split <- c(
  palm = gl("vo_rs_palm", final_year, "carbon_loss"),
  soy = gl("vo_rs_soy", final_year, "carbon_loss")
)
interaction_pct <- 100 * (gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") - sum(crop_split)) /
  gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss")

fmt1 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1, big.mark = ",")
fmt0 <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 0, big.mark = ",")

# Figures: one ggplot2 theme and one set of colors throughout. Scenarios and crops keep the same
# colors in every figure; magnitude on maps uses viridisLite's magma, reversed so darker means
# more loss (the ends are trimmed so the lightest step stays visible on the gray land).
col_surface <- "#fcfcfb"
col_land <- "#ecebe6"
col_scenario <- c(rs = "#2a78d6", model = "#eb6834")
scenario_labels <- c(rs = "Roberts & Schlenker", model = "Roberts & Schlenker demand, land-use model supply")
col_crop <- c("Oil palm" = "#1baf7a", "Soybeans" = "#eda100")
map_ramp <- function(n) viridisLite::magma(n, direction = -1, begin = 0.1, end = 0.95)

theme_report <- function() {
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    ggplot2::theme(
      plot.background = ggplot2::element_rect(fill = col_surface, colour = NA),
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_line(colour = "#e1e0d9", linewidth = 0.3),
      panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#52514e"),
      plot.title = ggplot2::element_text(colour = "#0b0b0b", face = "bold"),
      plot.title.position = "plot",
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "left"
    )
}
theme_map <- function() {
  theme_report() +
    ggplot2::theme(
      panel.grid.major = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.text = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      axis.title = ggplot2::element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom",
      legend.justification = "center"
    )
}

# Country outlines (Natural Earth 1:110m), as vertices; see r/make_basemap.R.
basemap <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "natural_earth", "ne_110m_admin_0_countries.csv.gz"))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Preliminary and exploratory: use with extreme caution

This is a prototype analysis. Treat every number in it as a rough indication of scale, not as an estimate for policy, regulation or carbon accounting. The numbers may change substantially as the work continues. The main reasons:

- **The price shock is approximate, and it drives everything else.** We size it with a linear formula meant for small changes, applied to a demand increase of about `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of the world vegetable-oil market. Our two scenarios raise prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`%, and their ILUC estimates differ by a factor of `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_model", headline_years) / il("vo_rs", headline_years))`.
- **The land-use model's own supply response is far smaller than published estimates** ([Methods](#sec-model-supply)). Our primary scenario uses a published supply elasticity, so it is not consistent with the model's own supply response. The alternative uses the model's own, which is consistent but assumes nothing else adds supply.
- **Country-level results are especially uncertain.** We use a single global supply elasticity and apply the same price increase in every country. In reality, how much supply responds, and how much of a world price change reaches local farmers, varies from country to country. The model also holds each country's recent deforestation conditions fixed, pools some small countries into regions, and gives each cell the crop mix of a broad zone, so our palm price shock reaches places where little palm is grown today ([Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix)).
- **Emissions are incomplete.** We count only carbon in forest biomass. Peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration are left out, which matters most in Indonesia and Malaysia. Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the land-use model.
- **The dynamics are simplified.** Prices jump once and stay there, and cleared forest never grows back.

[Caveats](#sec-caveats) lists these in more detail.
:::

## Summary

ICCT estimates that meeting the Net-Zero Framework's Base target at least cost would take about `r fmt0(shock_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters)` billion liters of virgin vegetable oil a year for marine renewable diesel by 2035 [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. That is `r fmt0(shock_2035$demand_share_pct)`% of current world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflower oil combined.

With Roberts & Schlenker's supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279], our primary case, that much extra demand raises vegetable-oil prices by `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. With their demand elasticity and the land-use model's own supply elasticity (`r formatC(shock_2035$eps_s_model, digits = 2, format = "fg")`, see [Methods](#sec-model-supply)), prices rise `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`%. In that case the model adds almost no new supply, so other buyers have to give up nearly all of the oil the ships use. Both numbers come from a linear approximation that works for small demand shifts, and this shift is large, so the exact percentages are rough. We use them to size the shocks we feed into the land-use model, not as price forecasts.

The land-use model prices palm as palm oil but soybeans as whole beans. About 35% of the value of a crushed soybean is oil and the rest is meal [@janzen2025, Fig. 2], so if meal prices hold steady, a `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% rise in the oil price raises the soybean price by about `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. The Roberts & Schlenker scenario therefore raises palm oil prices `r fmt0(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices `r fmt0(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%.

With those prices, emLab's land-use model clears an extra `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha of forest in the first 15 years compared with business as usual, releasing `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. Over the model's full `r n_years`-year run the totals are `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "area_loss") / 1e6)` Mha and `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂. With the land-use model's own supply elasticity, the full-run loss is `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs_model", final_year, "carbon_loss") / 1e9)` Gt CO₂, `r fmt1(gl("vo_rs_model", final_year, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss"))` times as much. In the Roberts & Schlenker scenario, the palm price increase causes `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["palm"]] / sum(crop_split))`% of the additional loss and the soybean increase `r fmt0(100 * crop_split[["soy"]] / sum(crop_split))`%. Most of it falls in a few countries: `r rs_final$country[1]` and `r rs_final$country[2]` account for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:2]))`%, and the top 12 countries for `r fmt0(100 * sum(rs_final$share[1:12]))`%. Treat this split with particular caution (see the box above).

Spread over `r headline_years` years of fuel use, the additional forest carbon loss in the Roberts & Schlenker scenario comes to `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g CO₂ per MJ of VO-RD (`r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 20))` over 20 years, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 30))` over 30), or `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_model", 25))` with the land-use model's own supply elasticity. Added to VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` g CO₂e/MJ [@seber2025, p. 6], the Roberts & Schlenker value gives `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))` g/MJ, `r ifelse(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25) < fossil_baseline_ci, "below", "above")` the `r fossil_baseline_ci` fossil baseline; the other value gives `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_model", 25))`, `r ifelse(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs_model", 25) < fossil_baseline_ci, "below", "above")` it.

ICCT has used an ILUC value of 62 g CO₂e/MJ [@sturrup2026, p. 10], and @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] estimate 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ for palm. Our Roberts & Schlenker value, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))` g/MJ, is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs", 25))`, and the value with the land-use model's own supply elasticity, `r fmt1(il("vo_rs_model", 25))`, is `r vs_benchmarks(il("vo_rs_model", 25))`. Both benchmarks are ILUC alone, like ours, and leave out the fuel's direct emissions. So ICCT's 62 compares with our `r fmt1(il("vo_rs", 25))`, not with our total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + il("vo_rs", 25))`; adding VO-RD's direct `r vord_direct_ci` to ICCT's 62 gives a total of `r fmt1(vord_direct_ci + 62)`. Our values count only carbon in forest biomass, which understates ILUC: peat alone was 614 of the 1,086 Tg CO₂e in Chen et al.'s estimate [@chen2026, Table 1, p. 13].

## Background

### The IMO Net-Zero Framework

In April 2025 the International Maritime Organization approved draft amendments to MARPOL Annex VI [@sturrup2026, p. 1] that would set binding greenhouse-gas fuel-intensity (GFI) targets for ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above. GFI is measured in well-to-wake g CO₂e/MJ against a 2008 baseline of 93.3 [@seber2025, p. 1]. There are two targets. The Base target tightens from a 4% reduction in 2028 to 30% by 2035, and the stricter Direct Compliance target from 17% to 43%. Ships above the Base target pay \$380 per tonne of excess CO₂e (Tier 2), and ships between the two targets pay \$100 per tonne (Tier 1) [@seber2025, pp. 1–2].

As of October 2026 the framework has not been adopted. At an extraordinary session in October 2025 that was called to adopt it, a Saudi Arabian motion to adjourn for a year passed with 57 votes. Those votes included 15 countries that had backed the framework in April 2025 [@carbonbrief2026]. At MEPC 84 (27 April–1 May 2026), the IMO's Marine Environment Protection Committee kept the April 2025 text as the basis for further work, let countries put forward alternatives, and scheduled two more meetings of its intersessional working group on greenhouse gases [@carbonbrief2026; @abs2026mepc84, p. 4]. The first of those meetings, ISWG-GHG 22 (1–4 September 2026), ended without agreement [@shipandbunker2026]. The sharpest split is over the GHG price and the central IMO fund that it pays into. By one observer's count of the countries that spoke, 38 supported them and 17, mostly oil producers, were against, and the United States repeated that it opposes any fund run by the IMO [@shipandbunker2026]. Also unresolved are how steep the GFI trajectory should be in the early years and how ships can pool and transfer compliance surpluses [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Japan's proposal to replace the fund with direct payments from shipowners got little support in September [@maritimeexecutive2026]. Japan has since tabled a revised version for the next round that drops the fund and has ships cover shortfalls by buying surplus units from other ships [@marineinsight2026].

The working group meets again 23–27 November, followed by MEPC 85 from 30 November to 3 December. If MEPC 85 agrees, the extraordinary session resumes on 4 December 2026, and the amendments could be put to a vote that day [@abs2026mepc84, p. 4; @shipandbunker2026]. Whatever is adopted may differ from the April 2025 text that this analysis starts from. A gentler early trajectory would mean less biofuel demand, and dropping the GHG price would change the compliance costs that decide the fuel mix.

Fuels are judged only on their direct life-cycle emissions, with nothing for land-use change. The IMO's life-cycle guidelines say ILUC estimates are too uncertain to give each fuel a number, so ILUC is handled through a qualitative risk-based approach instead [@imo2024lca, paras. 4.12–4.13]. MEPC 84 supported this approach in principle and asked for more quantitative analysis by MEPC 85 [@abs2026mepc84, p. 6]. Blending in biofuel costs less than the \$380 Tier 2 penalty, so the cheapest strategy is to blend just enough to meet the Base target. In ICCT's least-cost fuel mix, used-cooking-oil renewable diesel (UCO-RD) runs out at about 5% of shipping energy, and virgin vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) covers the rest, reaching 46% of shipping energy by 2035 [@seber2025, p. 4 and Table 1, p. 5].

ICCT's Table 1 gives that mix for each year from 2028 to 2035. We read it straight from the PDF; the last column, virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, is the demand shift used in this analysis.

```{r}
#| label: scrape-icct-table-1

pdf_path <- file.path(
  "data",
  "icct_biofuel_demand_report",
  "ID-450-Vegetable-Oil_research-brief_final.pdf"
)

# Extract page 5 as text and keep only the data rows (years 2028–2035)
page5 <- pdftools::pdf_text(pdf_path)[5]
lines <- stringr::str_trim(stringr::str_split(page5, "\n")[[1]])
data_lines <- stringr::str_subset(lines, "^20(2[89]|3[0-5])\\b")

# Each data row yields exactly 10 numeric tokens:
#   year, shipping demand, base target, fossil LNG %,
#   UCO-RD %, UCO-RD bl, VO-RD %, VO-RD bl, UCO demand bl, VO demand bl
nums <- stringr::str_extract_all(data_lines, "[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*")
mat <- do.call(rbind, lapply(nums, function(x) as.numeric(x[seq_len(10)])))

icct_table_1 <- tibble::as_tibble(mat, .name_repair = "minimal")
names(icct_table_1) <- c(
  "year",
  "shipping_energy_demand_ej",
  "base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj",
  "fossil_lng_pct",
  "ucord_pct_energy_demand",
  "ucord_billion_liters",
  "vord_pct_energy_demand",
  "vord_billion_liters",
  "uco_demand_billion_liters",
  "vo_demand_billion_liters"
)

icct_table_1 <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::mutate(year = as.integer(year)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(year)

# Saved for the setup chunk, which needs the 2035 VO-RD energy for the ILUC calculation.
utils::write.csv(icct_table_1, file.path("data", "derived", "icct_table_1.csv"), row.names = FALSE)

knitr::kable(
  icct_table_1 |>
    dplyr::select(
      year,
      shipping_energy_demand_ej,
      base_target_trajectory_gco2e_mj,
      ucord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_pct_energy_demand,
      vord_billion_liters,
      vo_demand_billion_liters
    ),
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "Shipping energy (EJ)",
    "Base target (g CO₂e/MJ)",
    "UCO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD (% of energy)",
    "VO-RD fuel (billion L)",
    "Virgin VO feedstock (billion L)"
  ),
  caption = "ICCT Table 1, selected columns [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Virgin vegetable-oil feedstock, the last column, is the demand shock D."
)
```

The direct carbon intensities behind the mix:

| Fuel | Life-cycle carbon intensity (g CO₂e/MJ) |
|---|---|
| 2008 baseline | 93.3 |
| Heavy fuel oil (HFO) | 92.8 |
| Fossil LNG | 85.7 |
| Soy vegetable-oil renewable diesel (VO-RD) | 42.3 |

### Indirect land-use change

Indirect land-use change (ILUC) happens when demand for a biofuel feedstock raises crop prices and the higher prices lead to forest being cleared for farmland somewhere else. These emissions fall outside the fuel's own supply chain, so a fuel mix can meet the GFI targets on paper while adding emissions that nobody counts. The steps in this analysis:

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  A["IMO Net-Zero Framework"] --> F["Marine VO-RD demand<br/><i>ICCT cost-optimization</i>"]
  F --> B["Virgin vegetable-oil demand<br/><i>1.22 kg oil per kg RD</i>"]
  B --> C["Vegetable-oil price shock<br/><i>this report</i>"]
  C --> D["Forest loss by country<br/><i>emLab land-use model</i>"]
  D --> E["ILUC carbon intensity<br/><i>this report</i>"]
```

ICCT converts renewable diesel to oil at 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel [@seber2025, p. 3, note 9].

Published ILUC estimates for vegetable-oil biofuels range widely:

| Source | Approach | ILUC result |
|---|---|---|
| ICCT climate & revenue brief [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11] | Fixed factor applied to ICCT's demand projection | 62 g CO₂e/MJ; ~285 Mt CO₂e/yr by 2035; ~950 Mt CO₂e over 2028–2035 |
| U.S. EPA model comparison [@epa2023mce, Table 7.7-1, p. 113] | Five models, soybean-oil biodiesel shock | Land-use change: 10 to 295 kg CO₂e/MMBTU (GCAM: 62) |
| @chen2026 [Table 1, p. 13] | Econometric estimates of demand → price → deforestation for palm, 2002–2018 | 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ (90% CI 48.7–113.5) |
| GLOBIOM for the EU [@valin2015, p. x] | Global economic land-use model, emissions spread over 20 years | 231 g CO₂e/MJ for palm oil, 150 for soybean oil |

: ICCT takes its 62 from the EPA model comparison [@sturrup2026, p. 10]. The only 62 in the EPA's results table is GCAM's land-use-change value, which is in kg CO₂e/MMBTU (≈ 59 g CO₂e/MJ), so we assume that is the source. Every value in the table is ILUC alone and leaves out the fuel's direct life-cycle emissions. ICCT adds its 62, weighted by VO-RD's share of shipping energy (62 × 46% ≈ 28.5 g CO₂e/MJ in 2035), to the fleet's Base-target GFI [@sturrup2026, pp. 10–11], and finds the ILUC-adjusted fleet GFI reaches 93.86 g CO₂e/MJ by 2035, above the fossil baseline [@sturrup2026, Table A1, p. 15].

Like Chen et al., we estimate how much the demand shift raises prices and then use an econometric land-use model to translate prices into forest loss, instead of assuming an ILUC factor.

## Methods and assumptions

The analysis has four steps:

1. Convert ICCT's 2035 vegetable-oil demand into a price shock, in two ways: with Roberts & Schlenker's supply and demand elasticities (our primary case), and with their demand elasticity and the land-use model's own supply elasticity.
2. Translate that shock into prices for the crops in emLab's land-use model.
3. Run the model with baseline and shocked prices, both at a zero carbon price, and take the difference in forest loss.
4. Spread the additional emissions over the fuel used, to get g CO₂ per MJ.

### From demand to a price shock {#sec-price-shock}

When demand shifts out, the equilibrium price rises by roughly the size of the shift divided by the difference between the supply and demand elasticities [@roberts2013, Table 1, panel C, p. 2279]:

$$ \%\Delta P \;\approx\; \underbrace{\frac{D}{Q_0}}_{\text{demand shift}} \;\times\; \underbrace{\frac{1}{\varepsilon_s - \varepsilon_d}}_{\text{multiplier } M} $$

where $D$ is marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, $Q_0$ is baseline world production, $\varepsilon_s > 0$ is the supply elasticity and $\varepsilon_d < 0$ is the demand elasticity.

| Input | Value | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Marine virgin vegetable-oil demand, 2035 ($D$) | 139.3 billion L | ICCT [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5] |
| Baseline market ($Q_0$) | ≈ 204 Mt: world production of palm, soybean, rapeseed and sunflowerseed oil, 2024/25 | USDA PSD [@usdapsd] |
| Oil density, to put $D$ and $Q_0$ in the same units | 0.92 kg/L | ICCT's own soy-oil conversion: 12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L (0.919 kg/L) [@seber2025, Table A1, p. 7] |
| Demand elasticity ($\varepsilon_d$) | −0.05 | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279] (range −0.03 to −0.07) |
| Supply elasticity, primary ($\varepsilon_s$) | 0.10 | @roberts2013 [Table 1, p. 2279] (range 0.09–0.12) |
| Supply elasticity, alternative ($\varepsilon_s$) | `r formatC(shock_2035$eps_s_model, digits = 2, format = "fg")`: the land-use model's own one-year supply elasticity for vegetable oil | Our estimate ([below](#sec-model-supply)) |
| Elasticities of Chen et al., for comparison only | $\varepsilon_s \approx 0.12$ (long-run 0.10 for palm and 0.13 for competing oil crops, weighted by production), $\varepsilon_d = -0.284$ (the inverse of a demand flexibility of −3.523) | @chen2026 [Fig. 2B, rows 3–4, p. 4; Table S1, col. 3] |
| Demand year | 2035 only | Our choice: the final year of the ICCT projection |
| "Beyond marginal" flag | demand share > 25% | Our own cutoff for where the approximation gets unreliable (not from a source) |

: Inputs to the price shock. The primary multiplier is $M \approx 6.7$; with the land-use model's supply elasticity, $M \approx 20$. Chen et al.'s elasticities would give $M \approx 2.5$.

$Q_0$ is world production of the four oils in 2024/25, summed across countries from the USDA Foreign Agricultural Service's PSD oilseeds data (`data/usda_psd_oilseeds/psd_oilseeds_csv.zip`, downloaded 2026-07-31) [@usdapsd]. USDA revises PSD continuously, so a later download may give slightly different numbers.

```{r}
#| label: psd-q0

psd_zip_path <- file.path("data", "usda_psd_oilseeds", "psd_oilseeds_csv.zip")
psd <- utils::read.csv(unz(psd_zip_path, "psd_oilseeds.csv"))

q0_market_year <- 2024 # marketing year 2024/25

psd_four_oils <- psd |>
  dplyr::filter(
    Commodity_Description %in%
      c("Oil, Palm", "Oil, Soybean", "Oil, Rapeseed", "Oil, Sunflowerseed"),
    Attribute_Description == "Production",
    Market_Year == q0_market_year
  ) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    production_mt = sum(Value) / 1000, # reported in 1000 MT
    .by = Commodity_Description
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(production_mt))
q0_mt <- sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt) # ~204 Mt

knitr::kable(
  psd_four_oils,
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c("Commodity", "World production, 2024/25 (million t)"),
  caption = paste0(
    "World production of the four major vegetable oils (USDA PSD). Total: ",
    round(sum(psd_four_oils$production_mt), 1),
    " million t."
  )
)
```

Some notes on these choices:

- Vegetable oils substitute for one another, so we treat them as one market even though the marine demand is for soy oil [@chen2026, p. 4]. Roberts & Schlenker's elasticities are for the world market in calories from maize, wheat, rice and soybeans, not for vegetable oils; we use them as a stand-in.
- We keep the supply elasticity in the multiplier. The land-use model takes prices as given, so the price we give it should already reflect the supply response. Leaving $\varepsilon_s$ out of the primary case would give $M = 20$ and triple the shock. The land-use model's own supply elasticity is so small that using it does almost the same thing.
- The formula is a first-order approximation, and from about 2032 marine demand is a large share of the market, so the 2035 shock gives the scale of the effect, not its exact size. Roberts & Schlenker also note that because the multiplier is a convex function of the elasticities, its expected value is higher than the value at the point estimates [@roberts2013, p. 2280], which points the same way.
- Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity is how much farmers expand output in response to the price expected at planting, a year ahead. They argue it is not just a short-run lower bound, because farmers expect price changes to persist [@roberts2013, p. 2285]. The land-use model's one-year elasticity is the comparable number. Oil palm takes about four years to start fruiting, so palm supply barely responds in the short run [@chen2026, p. 4].
- Crushing soybeans also produces meal, and meal revenue offsets some of the pressure on oil prices. Roberts & Schlenker cut their price effect by a third when a third of the calories come back as animal feed [@roberts2013, p. 2280]. We make no adjustment like this to the oil price, so on this count the shock is too high. (Meal does affect how the shock reaches the soybean price; see the next section.)
- The formula reproduces both source papers' headline price effects (see [Results](#sec-results-price)).

### The land-use model's own supply elasticity {#sec-model-supply}

The land-use model has a supply response of its own: a higher crop price raises a cell's potential revenue, more forest is cleared, and some of the cleared land grows the crop. To measure it, `r/land_use_model/00d_supply_curve.R` raises the palm oil price, the soybean price, or both (soybeans by $s$ times the palm change, as in the [mapping](#sec-mapping)) by between −50% and +1,500%, and simulates forward from 2020 at a zero carbon price. It turns the extra forest cleared relative to BAU into extra production the way the model's own code does (`endog_prices()` in `simulation_functions.R`): cleared area × the share of the cell's 2000–2020 forest loss that became cropland × the cell's crop mix × yield. Palm counts as palm oil and soybeans as beans; for vegetable oil we add the oil in the soybeans, at 11 lb per 60 lb bushel [@janzen2025, Fig. 2]. We divide by 2024/25 world production of palm oil, soybeans, and the four oils ($Q_0$) [@usdapsd], so the elasticities are on the same footing as the published ones.

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-curve
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

# Extra palm oil and soybean production on the extra forest cleared after a permanent price
# change, relative to BAU (r/land_use_model/00d_supply_curve.R), in each experiment's own
# commodity: palm oil, soybeans, or vegetable oil (palm oil plus the oil in the soybeans).
model_supply <- utils::read.csv(file.path("data", "derived", "land_use_supply_curve.csv"))
vo_rows <- model_supply$experiment == "vegetable_oil"
stopifnot(
  "00d_supply_curve.R must map the soybean shock with soy_oil_value_share" = isTRUE(all.equal(
    model_supply$pct_change_soy[vo_rows], soy_oil_value_share * model_supply$pct_change_palm[vo_rows]
  ))
)

soy_oil_per_bean <- 11 / 60 # lb of oil per 60 lb bushel (Janzen & Wang 2025)
psd_world_mt <- function(commodity) {
  sum(psd$Value[psd$Commodity_Description == commodity & psd$Attribute_Description == "Production" &
    psd$Market_Year == q0_market_year]) / 1000
}
world_mt <- c(palm = psd_world_mt("Oil, Palm"), soy = psd_world_mt("Oilseed, Soybean"), vegetable_oil = q0_mt)
to_mt <- function(experiment, palm_t, soy_t) {
  ifelse(experiment == "palm", palm_t,
    ifelse(experiment == "soy", soy_t, palm_t + soy_oil_per_bean * soy_t)
  ) / 1e6
}
model_supply <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    extra_mt = to_mt(experiment, extra_palm_oil_t, extra_soybeans_t),
    extra_mt_upper = to_mt(experiment, extra_palm_oil_t_upper, extra_soybeans_t_upper),
    pct_supply = 100 * extra_mt / world_mt[experiment],
    pct_supply_upper = 100 * extra_mt_upper / world_mt[experiment]
  )
supply_at <- function(exp, pct, yrs = 1) {
  model_supply[model_supply$experiment == exp & model_supply$pct_change == pct & model_supply$years == yrs, ]
}

# Point elasticities at baseline prices, from the -1% and +1% runs.
model_elasticity <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(abs(pct_change) == 1) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    eps = (pct_supply[pct_change == 1] - pct_supply[pct_change == -1]) / 2,
    eps_upper = (pct_supply_upper[pct_change == 1] - pct_supply_upper[pct_change == -1]) / 2,
    .by = c(experiment, years)
  )
eps_model <- function(exp, yrs = 1, col = "eps") {
  model_elasticity[[col]][model_elasticity$experiment == exp & model_elasticity$years == yrs]
}

crop_labels <- c(palm = "Palm oil (palm price)", soy = "Soybeans (soybean price)", vegetable_oil = "Vegetable oil (both prices)")
col_horizon <- c("1 year" = "#2a78d6", "25 years" = "#8f8d86")
curve_plot <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(years %in% c(1, 25)) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(expand.grid(experiment = names(crop_labels), years = c(1, 25), pct_change = 0, extra_mt = 0)) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    horizon = ifelse(years == 1, "1 year", "25 years"),
    panel = factor(crop_labels[experiment], levels = crop_labels)
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(experiment, years, pct_change)

ggplot2::ggplot(curve_plot, ggplot2::aes(extra_mt, pct_change, colour = horizon, linetype = horizon)) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b9", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#c3c2b9", linewidth = 0.4) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free_x") +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_horizon, name = "After the price change:") +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = c("1 year" = "solid", "25 years" = "22"), name = "After the price change:") +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_number(accuracy = 0.1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The land-use model's supply curves",
    x = "Extra production relative to BAU (Mt a year)",
    y = "Change in price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-elasticity

fmt_eps <- function(x) formatC(x, digits = 2, format = "fg")
knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Supply of" = c("Palm oil", "Soybeans", "Vegetable oil"),
    "Price changed" = c("Palm", "Soybeans", "Palm, and soybeans by s times as much"),
    "1 year" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 1)),
    "5 years" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 5)),
    "10 years" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 10)),
    "25 years" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 25)),
    "1 year, all cleared land cropped" = fmt_eps(sapply(names(crop_labels), eps_model, yrs = 1, col = "eps_upper")),
    "Published" = c("0.10 (Chen et al.)", "0.13 (Chen et al.)", "0.10 (Roberts & Schlenker)"),
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  row.names = FALSE,
  align = "llrrrrrr",
  caption = paste(
    "Supply elasticities of the land-use model at baseline prices, by time since a permanent price change,",
    "from ±1% price changes and 2024/25 world production. The 'all cleared land cropped' column counts every",
    "extra hectare cleared as cropland. Published: Chen et al.'s long-run elasticities for palm and for",
    "competing oil crops [@chen2026, Fig. 2B], and Roberts & Schlenker's for staple calories,",
    "which our primary case uses [@roberts2013, Table 1, p. 2279]."
  )
)

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-numbers
#| include: false

# Numbers for the text: first-year clearing under BAU and from a +1% vegetable-oil price change,
# and the share of that extra clearing the model counts as cropland.
bau_year1_ha <- sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) - sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2021])
veg_1pct <- supply_at("vegetable_oil", 1)
cropland_share <- veg_1pct$extra_mt / veg_1pct$extra_mt_upper
veg_max <- supply_at("vegetable_oil", max(model_supply$pct_change))
```

The model's one-year supply elasticity for vegetable oil is `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil"))`, about `r fmt0(signif(0.10 / eps_model("vegetable_oil"), 1))` times smaller than Roberts & Schlenker's 0.10. Four things keep it small:

- A 1% rise in vegetable-oil prices clears an extra `r fmt0(veg_1pct$extra_forest_loss_ha)` ha of forest in the first year. Under BAU the model clears `r fmt1(bau_year1_ha / 1e6)` Mha that year.
- Weighted by where the extra clearing happens, the model counts only about `r fmt0(100 * cropland_share)`% of it as cropland, and only the palm and soybean share of each cell's crop mix as palm and soybeans. Even if every extra hectare became cropland, the elasticity would be `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil", col = "eps_upper"))`.
- New cropland on cleared forest is the model's only supply channel. Higher yields, expansion onto land that isn't forest, switching crops on existing farmland, and rapeseed and sunflower are all missing. Published elasticities describe the market's total supply response across all of these.
- The model gives each cell the crop mix of its whole GAEZ zone, which fits a model built to price carbon against a cell's total revenue. For a price shock to palm and soybeans alone, it means palm is at most 17.5% of any cell's crop mix, even in Riau, a palm frontier in central Sumatra, so both the revenue change from a palm price rise and the palm counted on cleared land are small. Compared with Chen et al.'s econometric estimate, the palm supply from forest we get this way in Indonesia and Malaysia is about 100 times smaller. This is probably the largest factor, and it suggests that reading a crop supply elasticity off the model is not a use it was built for; see [Appendix C](#sec-crop-mix).

Supply builds up over time, because the higher price keeps clearing faster every year: after 25 years the elasticity is `r fmt_eps(eps_model("vegetable_oil", 25))`. The one-year curves flatten a little at high prices: the average elasticity over a +`r fmt0(veg_max$pct_change)`% price change is `r fmt_eps(veg_max$pct_supply / veg_max$pct_change)`.

Our alternative price shock uses the one-year vegetable-oil elasticity, at baseline prices, in place of Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity. It is the comparable number, since Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity is also a one-year response (see [above](#sec-price-shock)).


### Mapping the shock to the model's crops {#sec-mapping}

Following @chen2026 [p. 3], we apply the same percentage shock to all vegetable-oil prices. They find that palm oil prices respond to production shocks in competing oil crops about as strongly as to shocks in palm itself (their Fig. 2A, p. 4), and that the four oil prices move together in the long run, with cointegrating coefficients close to one (soybean 1.04, canola 1.01, sunflower 0.86) [@chen2026, Table S5]. Other work points the same way but adds detail: in an equilibrium model of world vegetable-oil markets, @cui2017 [abstract] find that soy oil diverted to US biodiesel is replaced mostly by palm oil, and @santeramo2017 [p. 13] estimates cross-price elasticities between individual oils and finds a mix of substitutes and complements that varies by oil and region. Oil-specific pass-through would be a reasonable refinement.

Of the land-use model's 17 crops, only two produce vegetable oil: `Oil, palm`, priced per tonne of palm oil, and `Soybeans`, priced per tonne of beans. According to a comment in upstream's `00c_run_cobweb.R` (Section 5), the model's baseline prices are observed 2020 prices: \$768/t for palm and \$415/t for soybeans. Both are within 2% of the World Bank's 2020 averages for palm oil (\$752/t) and soybeans (\$407/t). Soybean oil averaged \$838/t that year [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1].

| Model crop | Shock | Why | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Palm oil | $\%\Delta P$ | The model prices palm as oil | — |
| Soybeans | $s \times \%\Delta P$, with $s = 0.353$ | Oil is only part of a soybean's value, and we hold the meal price fixed. $s = \$4.72 / (\$4.72 + \$8.66)$, from the 2007–2025 average per-bushel values of soybean oil and meal | @janzen2025 [Fig. 2] (USDA AMS Illinois plant prices; 11 lb oil and 48 lb meal per bushel) |
| Rapeseed/canola, sunflower | not modeled | Not among the model's crops | — |

: How the oil-price shock enters the land-use model.

Two checks on $s$: Irwin's 2007–2017 averages (\$4.43 oil, \$8.33 meal) give 0.347 [@irwin2017, Fig. 3], and World Bank 2020 prices for soybean oil and meal (\$838/t and \$394/t) give 0.33 [@worldbank2022pink, p. 1]. The share moves around a lot week to week. It stayed between 25% and 35% over 2013–2020, has rarely been below 35% since, and briefly hit 50% in 2021 and 2025 [@janzen2025, Fig. 3]. It is an accounting share and says nothing about how soybean prices actually respond.

Rapeseed and sunflower are not in the model, so their land-use response is missing and ILUC is understated. We still define $Q_0$ over all four oils, since all four compete in one market; using palm and soy alone would inflate the demand share. In 2024/25, 86% of world rapeseed came from Canada, the EU, China, India, Australia and Russia, and 90% of sunflowerseed from Russia, Ukraine, the EU, Argentina, Kazakhstan and China [@usdapsd], so most of the missing response is probably outside tropical forests. We have not quantified it.

### The land-use model {#sec-land-use-model}

We use emLab's global deforestation model (`emlab-ucsb/land-based-solutions`), copied into this repository. [Appendix A](#sec-lum-changes) lists every change we made to it.

The model is a fractional logit (fixest, quasibinomial) of each grid cell's annual deforestation rate on potential agricultural revenue and the remaining share of tree cover, with cell and country-by-year fixed effects. It is estimated on 2001–2020 (29.1 million cell-years). A cell's revenue is crop price minus transport cost, times attainable yield, summed over the 17 crops using each crop's harvested share as weights and capitalized at 5%. Transport cost scales with travel time to port and the crude-oil price.

Starting from 2020 tree cover, the model steps forward one year at a time from 2021 to 2171 over 1,450,769 cells in 154 countries. Country effects are held at their 2016–2020 average, and cleared forest never grows back.

All runs use a zero carbon price. BAU uses 2020 prices. The Roberts & Schlenker run raises palm oil prices by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`% and soybean prices by `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs)`%. The run with the land-use model's own supply elasticity raises them by `r fmt1(shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`% and `r fmt1(soy_oil_value_share * shock_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model)`%. Two more runs apply the Roberts & Schlenker shock to palm and to soybeans separately, so the loss can be split by crop. Prices jump once, in the first model year, and stay there, so model year 2035 means 15 years after the shock rather than the calendar year.

Forest carbon (t CO₂) is tree cover times carbon density, and forest area (ha) is forest carbon divided by carbon density, using the model's own conversion. We count forest carbon lost as emissions, which leaves out peat, soil carbon and lost future sequestration. As a sanity check, the model has `r fmt0(sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 1e6)` Mha of forest in 2020, `r fmt0(100 * sum(bau$area_bau[bau$year == 2020]) / 4.06e9)`% of FAO's 4.06 billion ha [@fao2020fra, p. 1]; the two use different definitions of forest.

The model inputs are emLab's `land-based-solutions` data on Nextcloud (`data/parallelized/1_input/full`), which we read but never modify. The simulation outputs (about 7 GB) are not in the repository; `r/land_use_model/03_summarise_results.R` reduces them to country × scenario × year totals (`data/derived/land_use_country_results.csv.gz`) and 0.5° grid-square totals (`data/derived/land_use_grid_loss.csv.gz`), which this report reads. Map outlines are Natural Earth's 1:110m countries [@naturalearth], stored as plain coordinates by `r/make_basemap.R`.

### ILUC carbon intensity {#sec-iluc-method}

We spread the additional emissions over an accounting period of $T$ years of fuel use:

$$ \text{ILUC}_T = \frac{\Delta C(T)}{T \times E} $$

where $\Delta C(T)$ is the cumulative additional forest carbon loss $T$ years after the shock and $E$ is the energy in one year of VO-RD use at the 2035 level. $E$ is ICCT's 46.0% VO-RD share of 10.0 EJ of shipping energy, or 4.60 EJ [@seber2025, Table 1, p. 5]. Working forward from the feedstock instead (139.3 billion L of oil at 0.92 kg/L, 1.22 kg of oil per kg of fuel, and 43,980 MJ per tonne of fuel) gives 4.62 EJ [@seber2025, pp. 3 and 6, Table A1]. Because the model applies the 2035 demand level from its first year, $T$ years means $T$ years of fuel use at that level, not a span of calendar years.

There is no single convention for $T$. The EU uses 20 years [@valin2015, p. 3] and the US EPA 30 [@chen2026, p. 13]. We report 20, 25 and 30 years and use 25 as the headline. That is the period Chen et al. use, matching the typical oil palm replanting cycle [@chen2026, p. 13], so our number compares directly with their 84.1 g CO₂e/MJ. ICCT's 62 g CO₂e/MJ comes from the EPA's model comparison, which divides cumulative emissions over 2020–2050 by cumulative fuel use over the same years [@epa2023mce, pp. 83–84], so it is closest to our 30-year value.

The result counts only CO₂ from forest biomass. We split it by country using each country's share of the additional loss, and by crop using the palm-only and soy-only runs.

## Results

### Vegetable-oil price shock {#sec-results-price}

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-parameters

# Q0 (psd-q0 chunk) in billion liters at 0.92 kg/L, ICCT's own soy-oil conversion
# (12.4 Mt = 13.5 billion L, ICCT Table A1).
oil_density_kg_l <- 0.92
q0_billion_liters <- q0_mt / oil_density_kg_l # ~221 billion L

# Primary: Roberts & Schlenker (2013) staple-food elasticities (Table 1), for supply and demand.
eps_s_rs <- 0.10
eps_d_rs <- -0.05

# Alternative: the same demand elasticity with the land-use model's own one-year supply
# elasticity for vegetable oil (model-supply-curve chunk).
eps_s_model <- eps_model("vegetable_oil")

# For comparison only, not run through the land-use model: Chen et al. (2026). Demand: flexibility
# of -3.523 (Table S1 col 3) inverts to eps_d = -0.284. Supply: long-run 0.10 (palm) and 0.13
# (competing oil crops) (Fig. 2B rows 3-4), weighted by production share as in their eps_S formula.
demand_flexibility_chen <- -3.523
eps_d_chen <- 1 / demand_flexibility_chen
share_palm <- psd_four_oils$production_mt[
  psd_four_oils$Commodity_Description == "Oil, Palm"
] /
  q0_mt
eps_s_chen <- 0.10 * share_palm + 0.13 * (1 - share_palm)

# eps_d is negative, so the multiplier denominator is eps_s + |eps_d|.
m_rs <- 1 / (eps_s_rs - eps_d_rs) # ~6.7
m_model <- 1 / (eps_s_model - eps_d_rs) # ~20
m_chen <- 1 / (eps_s_chen - eps_d_chen) # ~2.5

# Check: the formula should recover each source paper's own headline price effect.
validation <- tibble::tribble(
  ~check                                                        , ~shock_pct , ~m     , ~reported                                  ,
  "Roberts & Schlenker (p. 2277): ethanol mandate = 5% of world calories" , 5.0 , m_rs , "about 30% (p. 2280); 5% x their Table 1 multipliers gives 29-39%",
  "Chen et al. (p. 3): biofuels used 8.5% of vegetable oil, 2002-2018" , 8.5 , m_chen , "21.2% (90% CI: 12.2-28.5%) (p. 3)"
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(implied_pct = round(shock_pct * m, 1)) |>
  dplyr::select(check, shock_pct, implied_pct, reported)

knitr::kable(
  validation,
  col.names = c(
    "Check",
    "Demand shift (% of market)",
    "Implied %ΔP (our formula)",
    "Paper's result"
  ),
  caption = paste0(
    "Multipliers: M = ", round(m_rs, 2), " (Roberts & Schlenker) and M = ", round(m_chen, 2),
    " (Chen et al.). With each paper's own elasticities, the formula recovers that paper's headline result."
  )
)
```

```{r}
#| label: derive-price-shock

# %ΔP_t = (D_t / Q0) * M, expressed as a percent. beyond_marginal flags years where the shift
# exceeds 25% of the market, outside the regime where the approximation is reliable.
price_shock <- icct_table_1 |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    year,
    vo_demand_billion_liters,
    demand_share_pct = 100 * vo_demand_billion_liters / q0_billion_liters,
    pct_delta_p_rs = demand_share_pct * m_rs,
    pct_delta_p_rs_model = demand_share_pct * m_model,
    beyond_marginal = demand_share_pct > 25
  )

knitr::kable(
  price_shock |>
    dplyr::mutate(beyond_marginal = ifelse(beyond_marginal, "yes", "")),
  digits = 1,
  col.names = c(
    "Year",
    "VO demand (billion L)",
    "Share of market (%)",
    "%ΔP, Roberts & Schlenker",
    "%ΔP, model supply",
    "Beyond marginal"
  ),
  caption = "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand. Both scenarios use Roberts & Schlenker's demand elasticity; 'model supply' uses the land-use model's own supply elasticity. Years marked 'beyond marginal' are outside the range where the linear approximation holds up."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: price-shock-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

price_shock_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "rs", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs),
  data.frame(year = price_shock$year, scenario = "model", pct = price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs_model)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(price_shock_long, ggplot2::aes(year, pct, colour = scenario, fill = scenario)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(shape = 21, size = 2.8, stroke = 0.8, colour = col_surface) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_scenario, breaks = names(col_scenario), labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = col_scenario, breaks = names(col_scenario), labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = price_shock$year) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "Vegetable-oil price shock from marine biofuel demand",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in vegetable-oil price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

```{r}
#| label: model-supply-demand
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 5

# The vegetable-oil market in 2035: Roberts & Schlenker demand (eps_d = -0.05) before and after
# ICCT's marine demand D, against Roberts & Schlenker's supply (eps_s = 0.10) and the land-use
# model's simulated one-year supply curve. All curves use the price-shock formula's linear
# approximation, %dQ = eps x %dP. The marked equilibria are the price shocks run through the model.
shock_rs <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs[price_shock$year == 2035]
shock_model <- price_shock$pct_delta_p_rs_model[price_shock$year == 2035]
d_mt <- price_shock$vo_demand_billion_liters[price_shock$year == 2035] * oil_density_kg_l
veg_1y <- model_supply |>
  dplyr::filter(experiment == "vegetable_oil", years == 1) |>
  dplyr::select(pct_change, extra_mt) |>
  dplyr::bind_rows(data.frame(pct_change = 0, extra_mt = 0)) |>
  dplyr::arrange(pct_change)
model_supply_mt <- stats::approxfun(veg_1y$pct_change, veg_1y$extra_mt)

# Where the simulated curve itself crosses 2035 demand: extra supply equals marine demand minus the
# other demand the price rise chokes off.
p_cross_model <- stats::uniroot(
  \(p) model_supply_mt(p) - (d_mt + eps_d_rs * q0_mt * p / 100),
  range(veg_1y$pct_change)
)$root

curve_names <- c(
  "Demand today (ε = −0.05)",
  "Demand with 2035 marine demand",
  "Supply, Roberts & Schlenker (ε = 0.10)",
  paste0("Supply, land-use model (1 year, ε = ", fmt_eps(eps_s_model), ")")
)
p_grid <- seq(-50, 1500, by = 10)
market_curves <- rbind(
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[1], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[2], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * p_grid / 100) + d_mt),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[3], p = p_grid, q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_s_rs * p_grid / 100)),
  data.frame(curve = curve_names[4], p = veg_1y$pct_change, q = q0_mt + veg_1y$extra_mt)
)
market_curves$curve <- factor(market_curves$curve, levels = curve_names)
equilibria <- data.frame(
  q = q0_mt * (1 + eps_d_rs * c(0, shock_rs, shock_model) / 100) + c(0, d_mt, d_mt),
  p = c(0, shock_rs, shock_model),
  label = c("Today", paste0("+", fmt0(shock_rs), "%"), paste0("+", fmt0(shock_model), "%")),
  hjust = c(-0.3, -0.3, -0.3)
)

ggplot2::ggplot(market_curves, ggplot2::aes(q, p, colour = curve, linetype = curve)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    shape = 21, size = 3, fill = "#0b0b0b", colour = col_surface, stroke = 0.8
  ) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(
    data = equilibria, ggplot2::aes(q, p, label = label, hjust = hjust), inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3.4, colour = "#0b0b0b"
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(
    values = stats::setNames(c("#8f8d86", "#0b0b0b", col_scenario[["rs"]], col_scenario[["model"]]), curve_names),
    name = NULL
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_linetype_manual(values = stats::setNames(c("22", "solid", "solid", "solid"), curve_names), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::label_comma(suffix = "%")) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(100, 400, 100)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(40, 410), ylim = c(-50, 1500), expand = FALSE) +
  ggplot2::guides(colour = ggplot2::guide_legend(ncol = 2), linetype = ggplot2::guide_legend(ncol = 2)) +
  ggplot2::labs(
    title = "The world vegetable-oil market in 2035",
    x = "Vegetable oil (Mt a year)",
    y = "Change in vegetable-oil price"
  ) +
  theme_report()
```

The figure shows the 2035 market with Roberts & Schlenker's demand curve, before and after ICCT's marine demand of `r fmt0(d_mt)` Mt, and both supply curves. With Roberts & Schlenker's supply elasticity, the price rises `r fmt0(shock_rs)`%. Along the land-use model's supply curve, new supply covers almost none of the new demand, so the price has to rise until other buyers give up nearly all of it. That takes a rise of `r fmt0(shock_model)`%, a multiplier of `r fmt1(m_model)`, close to the demand-only limit of $1/|\varepsilon_d| = 20$. The simulated curve itself crosses the demand curve at `r fmt0(p_cross_model)`%, so using the elasticity at baseline prices makes little difference. Neither shock is a forecast. The demand shift is far outside the range where the linear formula holds, and with elasticities this small the answer depends mostly on the shape assumed for the curves. For comparison, Chen et al.'s elasticities would give `r fmt0(price_shock$demand_share_pct[price_shock$year == 2035] * m_chen)`% ($M \approx$ `r fmt1(m_chen)`).

The land-use runs use the 2035 values.

```{r}
#| label: export-price-shock

# Hand-off to the land-use model (full precision, no rounding). 01_prepare_data.R reads
# vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv. The elasticities are saved alongside for the Summary and Methods.
handoff_2035 <- price_shock |>
  dplyr::filter(year == 2035) |>
  dplyr::mutate(eps_d = eps_d_rs, eps_s_rs = eps_s_rs, eps_s_model = eps_s_model)

dir.create(file.path("data", "derived"), showWarnings = FALSE, recursive = TRUE)
utils::write.csv(
  handoff_2035,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)
utils::write.csv(
  price_shock,
  file.path("data", "derived", "vegetable_oil_price_shock.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

# The setup chunk read this file for the text above, before this render rewrote it. If it was out
# of date, that text used old numbers: stop so the report is rendered again.
if (!isTRUE(all.equal(shock_2035, as.data.frame(handoff_2035), check.attributes = FALSE))) {
  stop("vegetable_oil_price_shock_2035.csv was out of date and has been rewritten. Render again.")
}

cat(sprintf(
  paste0(
    "2035: VO demand %.0f billion L on a Q0 of %.0f billion L (demand share %.0f%%).\n",
    "Roberts & Schlenker: multiplier %.2f, price shock +%.0f%%.\n",
    "Land-use model supply: multiplier %.2f, price shock +%.0f%%."
  ),
  handoff_2035$vo_demand_billion_liters,
  q0_billion_liters,
  handoff_2035$demand_share_pct,
  m_rs,
  handoff_2035$pct_delta_p_rs,
  m_model,
  handoff_2035$pct_delta_p_rs_model
))
```

### Forest loss {#sec-results-forest}

Additional loss is the difference between forest in the BAU run and in a shocked run. It is cumulative, so the value in the last model year is the total additional loss over the whole simulation.

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-global

horizons <- c(2035, 2050, final_year)
global_table <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(year %in% horizons) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year),
    carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9,
    area_mha = area_loss / 1e6,
    pct_of_bau_carbon = 100 * carbon_loss / carbon_bau
  )

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    "Years after shock" = global_table$years_after_shock[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: Mha" = global_table$area_mha[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "R&S: % of BAU forest carbon" = global_table$pct_of_bau_carbon[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs"],
    "Model supply: Gt CO₂" = global_table$carbon_gt[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs_model"],
    "Model supply: Mha" = global_table$area_mha[global_table$scenario == "vo_rs_model"],
    check.names = FALSE
  ),
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Cumulative additional forest loss relative to BAU, all countries."
)
```

```{r}
#| label: forest-loss-timeseries
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4

global_ts <- global_loss |>
  dplyr::filter(scenario %in% c("vo_rs", "vo_rs_model")) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    years_after_shock = year - min(lum$year),
    scenario = ifelse(scenario == "vo_rs", "rs", "model"),
    carbon_gt = carbon_loss / 1e9
  )

ggplot2::ggplot(global_ts, ggplot2::aes(years_after_shock, carbon_gt, colour = scenario)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = col_scenario, breaks = names(col_scenario), labels = scenario_labels, name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 150, 25), expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))) +
  ggplot2::scale_y_continuous(expand = ggplot2::expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  ggplot2::labs(

    x = "Years after the price shock",
    y = expression("Gt CO"[2])

```

About half of the full-run loss happens in the first 15 years: `r fmt0(100 * gl("vo_rs", 2035, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs", final_year, "carbon_loss"))`% in the Roberts & Schlenker scenario and `r fmt0(100 * gl("vo_rs_model", 2035, "carbon_loss") / gl("vo_rs_model", final_year, "carbon_loss"))`% with the land-use model's own supply elasticity. The maps, charts and country table below show the Roberts & Schlenker scenario.

#### Where the loss falls

```{r}

Where the model pools neighboring countries into one region, each member shows the region's total; all such regions lose less than 1 Mt CO₂."

  dplyr::filter(carbon_loss > 0) |>
